articles.topic: Caffeine activates ancient cellular energy pathways
articles.headline: Your Morning Coffee Might Be Flipping a 500-Million-Year-Old Cellular Switch
articles.body: Scientists from Queen Mary University of London found that caffeine does far more than wake you up. The compound activates AMPK, an ancient cellular energy sensor that governs DNA repair, stress resistance, and cellular growth. The research, published in Microbial Cell, shows caffeine works through this pathway to influence processes directly linked to aging. When cells run low on fuel, AMPK kicks in to help them adapt. The study suggests caffeine's proven connection to healthier aging now has a cellular mechanism behind it. This discovery opens doors to understanding how dietary compounds influence longevity and aging at the most fundamental level.
articles.takeaway: Your daily coffee habit might be triggering cellular repair systems linked to longevity. The benefit comes through AMPK activation, not just caffeine's stimulant effect.
articles.source: ScienceAlert / Queen Mary University of London

articles.topic: Semaglutide reduces psychiatric hospitalizations in bipolar
articles.headline: Weight Loss Drug Linked to 21% Lower Risk of Psychiatric Crisis
articles.body: A large Swedish study tracking nearly 15,000 people with bipolar disorder found something unexpected: semaglutide (Ozempic/Wegovy) was associated with a 21% lower risk of psychiatric hospitalization. Researchers compared each person against themselves, looking at hospitalization rates during periods when they were taking the drug versus when they weren't. The effect was specific to semaglutide—other GLP-1 drugs didn't show the same pattern. Scientists believe GLP-1 signaling may protect the brain by reducing inflammation and cellular stress, pathways linked to mood instability. This suggests weight-loss medications might have psychiatric benefits beyond metabolic health, though more research is needed.
articles.takeaway: If you have bipolar disorder and are considering GLP-1 therapy, the data suggests potential mood-stabilizing benefits alongside weight management. Discuss with your psychiatrist.

articles.topic: Depression disrupts brain's neuron production capacity
articles.headline: Depression May Be Shutting Down Your Brain's Ability to Repair Itself
articles.body: A groundbreaking Columbia University study found that adults with depression show disrupted production of new neurons in the hippocampus, potentially weakening the brain's ability to process and separate new experiences from painful memories. Researchers examined nearly half a million brain cells and found molecular disruptions throughout the entire memory circuit. Depression doesn't just affect mood—it impairs the brain's fundamental capacity to create new neurons, which appears crucial for cognitive flexibility and emotional recovery. The findings suggest that reactivating neurogenesis could open new treatment pathways. The research also identified specific molecular changes that might allow future therapies tailored to individual forms of depression.
articles.takeaway: New treatments targeting neurogenesis could one day reverse depression's effects on the brain's capacity to adapt and recover. This explains why depression feels cognitively trapping.
articles.source: Nature Medicine / Columbia University Irving Medical Center

articles.topic: Gut bacteria transfer between people across continents
articles.headline: Your Gut Bacteria Might Be Spreading Faster Than You Think
articles.body: University of Vienna researchers discovered that some gut bacterial populations can spread rapidly between people and even across continents, suggesting the microbiome is far more transmissible than previously thought. Using reverse ecology methods, they found that many familiar gut bacterial species actually consist of separate evolutionary groups, each adapted to different conditions. Certain strains linked to aging, inflammatory bowel disease, colorectal cancer, and type 2 diabetes were identified spreading globally. Researchers documented over 10 million instances of bacterial strain sharing between mothers and infants, household members, and communities. This finding reshapes how scientists think about microbiome composition—it's not just shaped by diet and lifestyle, but by active transmission between people.
articles.takeaway: Your microbiome is more influenced by who you live with and interact with regularly than previously understood. Proximity matters more than we realized.

workout.title: Band-Assisted Pull-Up Foundation: Scapular Strength & Lat Activation
workout.tip: Before pulling, practice 5 dead hangs (5–10 seconds each) to activate your lats and shoulders. Think 'elbows to hips' rather than 'hands to chest' — this cue locks in proper lat recruitment and prevents arm dominance.
workout.warmup: 5 min: 10 arm circles forward & backward, 10 band pull-aparts (light resistance), 5 scapular pulls on bar (no leg drive), 10 shoulder rolls, 3 assisted dead hangs (3–5 sec each)

exercises.name: Band-Assisted Pull-Ups
exercises.notes: Loop medium or heavy band under feet; grip shoulder-width, pull elbows down and back, pause 1 sec at top. Band reduces load while you build strength. If too difficult, use thicker band; if too easy, use thinner band next week.

exercises.name: Dumbbell Single-Arm Row (Tempo)
exercises.notes: 2-second eccentric (lower), row to hip, squeeze scapula at top. This unilateral work corrects imbalances and reinforces single-side lat activation. Keep torso stable—don't twist.

exercises.name: Face Pulls with Resistance Band
exercises.notes: Anchor band at eye level, pull elbows high and wide, externally rotate shoulders at end range. This strengthens rear delts and upper back, critical for posture correction and shoulder health.

exercises.name: Scapular Pulls (Dead Hang Activation)
exercises.notes: Hang on bar, depress scapula (pull shoulders down), then elevate (shrug). No leg drive, no full pull-up—just scapular movement. Builds foundational lat and rhomboid control.

workout.cooldown: 5 min: dead hang 15 sec, chest doorway stretch 20 sec each side, lat stretch (arm overhead, gentle side bend) 20 sec each side, shoulder external rotation (band or towel) 15 sec each side
workout.description: A beginner-friendly pull progression using band assistance to build scapular stability, lat engagement, and pulling mechanics. This session teaches proper shoulder positioning and progressively reduces dependency on band support through targeted lat rows and activation drills. Perfect for busy professionals establishing a solid pulling foundation before advancing to harder progressions.

meal.title: Soft Polenta with Poached Eggs, Spinach & Roasted Cherry Tomatoes
meal.description: Creamy, slow-cooked polenta provides sustained carbohydrate energy for endurance training, while the poached eggs deliver choline for muscle coordination and two-day storage stability. Spinach and tomatoes round out the nutrient profile without adding heaviness.
ingredients: 2 cups fresh spinach (or 1 cup frozen, thawed)
Sea salt, black pepper, and red pepper flakes to taste
meal.instructions:
1. Toss cherry tomatoes with ½ tbsp olive oil, salt, and pepper. Spread on a sheet pan and roast at 400°F for 12–15 minutes until blistered and caramelized.
2. While tomatoes roast, bring milk and stock to a simmer in a medium saucepan over medium heat.
3. Slowly whisk in polenta cornmeal, stirring constantly to avoid lumps. Reduce heat to low and cook for 8–10 minutes, stirring frequently, until creamy and thick.
4. Stir in butter, Parmesan, salt, and pepper. Taste and adjust seasoning.
5. Heat ½ tbsp olive oil in a separate skillet over medium heat. Add garlic and fresh spinach, sautéing for 2 minutes until wilted. Season with salt and pepper.
6. To poach eggs: bring a pot of water to a gentle simmer, add vinegar. Create a gentle whirlpool and slide one egg into the center; cook 3 minutes for runny yolk. Repeat with second egg.
7. Divide polenta between bowls, top with wilted spinach and roasted tomatoes, and carefully place one poached egg on each. Garnish with red pepper flakes.
meal.tip: Make polenta ahead on Sunday—it keeps 4 days refrigerated and reheats beautifully with a splash of milk. Roast the tomatoes the night before, and simply wilt fresh spinach and poach eggs the morning of for a restaurant-quality 8-minute finish.
